title: Frontend bundle size doubled after a dependency change
description: Problem: Frontend bundle size doubled after a dependency change. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: A developer upgrades a date-picker library to fix a bug, and the production JavaScript bundle jumps from one hundred fifty kilobytes to over three hundred. Page load slows, Time to Interactive regresses, and the team needs to ship a fix before the next release. This is a dependency hygiene and build-configuration problem.
How a dependency change can bloat the bundle

items: The new version no longer supports tree shaking and includes side effects at the package root.
The dependency replaces a small utility with a larger framework or brings in peer dependencies you did not install.
A barrel file re-exports the entire library, causing the bundler to include modules you never use.
The package ships CommonJS and ESM builds, and the bundler picks the wrong format.
New transitive dependencies add polyfills, locales, or styles that end up in the client bundle.
Source maps or type definitions are bundled by mistake because of a misconfigured entry.

terms.definition: Dead-code elimination that removes unused exports during the build. Requires ES modules and sideEffects flag.
An index.js or index.ts file that re-exports many modules, often causing bundlers to pull in entire libraries.
A file emitted by the bundler, such as a JavaScript bundle, that contains code from one or more modules.
The process of inspecting a built bundle to see which modules contribute the most to its size.

data.text: Run the bundle analyzer before and after the change. Most bundlers have a plugin or CLI flag that produces a treemap. Look for the new package or one of its transitive dependencies in the largest modules list. If the package is listed but you only use one function, the import path is likely the problem.

data.title: Peer dependencies are not automatic
data.text: If a package moves a dependency from bundled to peer, you must install it yourself. Forgetting to install the peer dependency can cause the bundler to inline a fallback, silently inflating the bundle.

data.caption: Investigating a bundle size regression
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Bundle size doubled] --> B[Run bundle analyzer]
    B --> C{New large module found?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Check import style: barrel vs deep]
    C -->|No| E[Check transitive dependencies]
    D --> F{Deep import available?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Switch to deep import]
    F -->|No| H[Consider lighter alternative]
    E --> I{Peer dependency missing?}
    I -->|Yes| J[Install peer dependency explicitly]
    I -->|No| K[Check sideEffects flag]
    G --> L[Rebuild and measure]
    H --> L
    J --> L
    K --> L
    L --> M{Size back to baseline?}
    M -->|Yes| N[Ship and add bundle budget]
    M -->|No| O[Add dependency size to CI checks]

items.question: Should I block all large dependencies in CI?
items.answer: Yes. Set a bundle-size budget in your bundler or CI script. When a PR exceeds the budget, it fails before merge. This catches regressions early instead of in production.

items.question: Why does a deep import not always work?
items.answer: Some libraries do not publish deep import paths, or their internal structure changes between versions. Check the library documentation, and use barrel imports only when the bundle size is acceptable.

items.question: How do I handle dependencies that cannot be tree-shaken?
items.answer: Replace them with a modular alternative, load them dynamically with import(), or accept the cost and document it as an intentional trade-off in your architecture decision record.

data.title: Investigate a bundle size regression
data.description: Simulate a dependency change and use bundle analysis to find and fix the culprit.
steps: Build the project and record current bundle sizes.
Upgrade a small dependency to a newer major version.
Rebuild and compare sizes with the analyzer.
Identify the module that grew the most and inspect its imports.
Apply a fix: deep import, dynamic import, or replacement.
Rebuild and confirm the size regression is resolved.
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to explain why the bundle grew, which import or transitive dependency caused it, and how you prevented it from happening again in CI.

data.title: Summary
points: Run bundle analysis in CI so size regressions are caught before production.
Prefer deep imports over barrel imports when the library supports them.
Check peer dependencies and sideEffects flags when upgrading packages.
Use dynamic import() for code-splitting non-critical dependencies.
Document intentional bundle cost in architecture decision records
data.takeaway: Bundle size is a shared responsibility. Every dependency upgrade should be reviewed for size, not just for features and bug fixes.
